analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare and raises federal Medicaid matching rates for those services.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote, after drawing just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare today excludes most dental, routine vision, and hearing care, so seniors pay out of pocket for cleanings, fillings, glasses, and hearing aids, or buy separate private plans. This bill would have added those services to Medicare — cleanings, fillings, root canals, dentures, eye exams, eyeglasses, contact lenses, hearing exams, and hearing aids — and would have raised the federal Medicaid match to 90% when states cover dental, vision, and hearing care for adults. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who currently pay the full cost of dental care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids themselves, and low-income adults on Medicaid in states where dental, vision, and hearing coverage is thin, because the federal government would cover 90% of those costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds routine dental cleanings and exams, basic and major dental services, emergency dental care, and dentures to Medicare's covered benefits.

It adds routine eye exams, eyeglasses, contact lenses, and low-vision devices, plus routine hearing exams and hearing aids, to Medicare coverage, repealing the statutory exclusions that currently bar payment for them.
It raises the federal share of Medicaid spending on dental, vision, and hearing services to 90%, making it much cheaper for states to cover those services for adult beneficiaries.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, through higher Medicare and Medicaid spending; the bill text contains no funding mechanism or revenue offset for the new benefits. Medicare beneficiaries would also owe coinsurance: at full phase-in the program pays 80% of the payment amount, leaving a 20% share for the patient.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal budget and Medicare cost-sharing

drawbacks.text: The benefit phases in slowly: Medicare's payment rate starts at 0% in the first year and rises 10 percentage points a year, reaching the full 80% rate only in the eighth year after enactment, so the newest benefit years leave the largest patient cost-share.

Coverage comes with limits: two cleanings and two routine exams per year, one full upper and lower denture set every five years, one pair of eyeglass lenses per year with frames every two years, a $200 cap on contact lenses over two years, and one hearing aid per ear every four years, and the Secretary may add prior-authorization requirements.
The bill text includes no revenue source or budget offset for the added Medicare and Medicaid spending, so it would have increased federal deficits unless paired with funding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For older and low-income Americans the gain is real: out-of-pocket costs for dentures, glasses, and hearing aids — which regularly run into the thousands of dollars — would eventually be largely covered. The offsetting costs are the federal price tag with no funding attached and a benefit design that takes most of a decade to reach meaningful payment levels and still leaves a 20% patient share.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Casey introduced the bill on May 13, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee markup, no committee report, and no floor vote, so the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill attracted a single cosponsor, Senator Cardin of Maryland, in addition to Senator Casey.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and Medicaid enrollees gained nothing, because the coverage never happened. Insurers selling standalone dental, vision, and hearing plans to seniors kept that market to themselves, and the federal budget avoided the cost of the new benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supplemental-plan insurers and the federal budget

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remaining nineteen months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever held, so the record shows only Democratic support and no recorded opposition either way.

industries.industry: Insurers selling standalone dental, vision, and hearing plans to seniors
industries.note: A Medicare benefit for these services would substitute for the private supplemental plans that currently sell seniors dental, vision, and hearing coverage. The bill died, so that market was left intact.
The bill creates a large pool of Medicare-covered dental patients paying a fraction of their own bill. Their interest in the bill runs alongside patients who currently skip care for cost.
Medicare coverage of hearing aids, reimbursed at up to 80%, would give the industry millions of covered customers whose hearing aids currently cost them thousands out of pocket.
Covered eye exams, eyeglasses, and contact lenses create new reimbursed demand, while patients gain access they now pay for privately.
A 90% federal match makes covering dental, vision, and hearing care for adults far cheaper for states, encouraging expanded coverage for low-income adults.
